title: Autostorager manual
what: It watches one folder and hands every G-code or bgcode file that appears in it to the server's storage. There the file is treated like a manual upload: the server reads its slicer details, draws its preview and lists it under Storage. The module never writes into the storage directly; it goes through the same API an upload uses.
flow1: The folder is read every few seconds, and only .gcode and .bgcode files are taken.
flow2: A file is read only after its size held still across two checks, so a file a slicer is still writing is left alone.
flow3: The module asks the storage for a free name and adds -1, -2 and so on if the name is taken.
flow4: The bytes are copied into the storage. Only after that copy is committed is the source moved into successful/.
flow5: A file that cannot be imported is moved into failed/, and a text file beside it says at which step it stopped and why.
linuxTitle: The folder on Linux, with the server in a container
linux: A container sees only what is mounted into it. Create the folder on the host, add it as a volume to the server's compose file, and enter the path inside the container on the settings page, not the host path.
linuxPath: In the example the host folder /srv/autostorager appears as /incoming in the container, so the setting is /incoming. Mount as many host folders as you want to supervise, up to four. The module creates successful/ and failed/ inside each supervised folder; on the host they appear as /srv/autostorager/successful and /srv/autostorager/failed.
other: There the server is a normal process and the folder is read directly. Enter the full path, such as C:\Autostorager or /Users/you/Autostorager. No mount is involved.
settingFolder: Supervised folders: up to four absolute paths, added with [+] New supervised directory. Each folder is watched on its own and keeps its own successful/ and failed/. No folder means nothing is watched.
settingInterval: Check interval in seconds: how often the folder is read. 60 s is one minute. A very short interval means constant requests, which costs I/O on a network share; five seconds is enough for most folders, and a file is noticed within about one interval.
settingStorage: Storage: which storage instance the file is imported into. Most servers have one, called local.
settingSize: Largest file in megabytes, 250 by default. A larger file is not imported; it goes to failed/ with the reason.
settingMove: Move on success: when on, the source is moved into successful/ after the import. When off, it stays where it was, and the next check would import it again under a new name.
names: A name already present in the storage is never overwritten. The module tries the same name with -1, then -2, and so on until the storage answers that the name is free.
failed: The source goes to failed/, and beside it a file named <file>-failure.txt names the step, the reason, the time and the path. The same line appears under Recent imports on the settings page.
precedence: The settings page and the module's own dashboard page can both carry these values. What is saved on the settings page wins, because it is stored in the module's database and survives a restart.
check: Drop a small .gcode into the folder. Within about one interval it should disappear from there, appear as successful/ inside the folder, and show up under Storage in the server with its preview. The Recent imports list on the settings page tells the same story.
smbTitle: The easy way: a folder on the server, mounted on your computer
smb: Create a folder on the server and share it. Mount that share on your computer, where it appears as a normal drive or folder: Y: on Windows, /mnt/y on Linux, smb://server/share on macOS. Enter the server path of that folder here, then save your prints into it from the slicer. The module imports them from there and moves them into successful/ inside the same share. If the server runs in a container, enter the path inside the container, not the host path.
localTitle: If the server runs on the same computer
local: Then nothing is shared and nothing is mounted. Create a folder such as ~/Autostorager or C:\Autostorager, enter its path here, and save your prints into it. That is the whole setup.
pathTitle: What to enter as the supervised folder
path: The field takes the path as the server sees it, not as your computer sees it. Without a container that is the folder itself, such as /srv/autostorager. In a container it is the path inside the container. In this example /app/config/pc-in is a container path: the host folder is pc-in inside the server's config directory, and that directory is mounted into the container as /app/config. Your own folders and mount points are your own; what matters is that the path exists where the container looks. Your computer's drive letter or /mnt path is never the value to enter here.

hostSettingsTitle: The settings in the extension's Settings tab
hostSettings: The server keeps a Settings tab for every extension. It carries the same values as this page and two more: language and message. What is saved on the Autostorager page wins, because it is stored in the module's database.
hostLanguage: language: system follows the browser, or en, de or cs. The language section below explains it.
hostMessage: message: the line the module's own route answers with. It is not drawn on the page; leave it unless a tool reads the route.
hostDefaults: interval_seconds, storage, max_mb, move_on_success: the defaults the module starts with. The values saved on the Autostorager page win.
captionSettings: The Settings tab of Autostorager on the server, with language, message and the other defaults.
language: The language is set on the server, not on this page: Extensions, Autostorager, Settings, the field language. system means the language the browser asks for; en, de or cs pin one. Czech is cs, not cz, though a country code is accepted as a courtesy.
languageRestart: The choice is saved at once and read at start-up, so the module restarts when it is saved. Pick a quiet moment: an import halfway through is cut off by that restart. A language this package does not carry falls back to the browser's, and from there to English. The buttons above switch the language for this visit without saving anything.
languageContribute: Want your own language? Copy locales/en.json and manual/en.json to <tag>.json, translate the values, keep the keys, open a pull request. Nobody here should write a language they do not speak, and a machine translation reads like one. The Czech is exactly that: a trial balloon, translated by a machine. Whether it holds up is for Czech readers to say.
